It is a privilege to share Persistent Systems’ 36th Annual Report. Each year provides an opportunity to pause in gratitude, reflect on how far we have come, and consider the changing world around us. Above all, it is an opportunity to acknowledge the trust that has made this journey possible.

It is a privilege to share Persistent Systems’ 36th Annual Report. Each year provides an opportunity to pause in gratitude, reflect on how far we have come, and consider the changing world around us. Above all, it is an opportunity to acknowledge the trust that has made this journey possible.
Over the years, organisations have used software to streamline processes, improve efficiency and create consistency. AI introduces a new possibility: systems that can assist in interpretation, judgement and decision- making. We are entering a period in which intelligence itself is becoming a technology platform. The transition from automation to intelligence is now underway, and its implications extend far beyond technology. It will influence how organisations operate, innovate and compete.
When we started Persistent in 1990, we had very limited resources. What we did have was curiosity, determination and a willingness to learn. We believed that if we remained useful to our customers and continued to create value for them, the business would grow. More than three decades later, those fundamentals remain unchanged.

Trust of this kind is never built in boardrooms alone. It is earned every day through the actions of our people. It is built project by project, commitment by commitment, often quietly and away from public view. Behind every customer relationship are teams that work diligently to solve problems, meet commitments and go the extra mile when needed. Their dedication, professionalism and care have helped Persistent earn the confidence of customers around the world, and I remain deeply grateful for their contribution.
While much of the current discussion focuses on foundation models and their rapidly advancing capabilities, I believe the long- term value of AI will be determined not by the models themselves, but by how effectively organisations combine intelligence with their own data, knowledge and experience. Over time, powerful models will become increasingly accessible. The more important differentiator will be context: an organisation’s enterprise data, customer relationships, business processes, operating history and accumulated expertise. Enterprises that successfully combine AI with this context will create advantages that are difficult to replicate.
Message from the Chairman

Message from the Chairman
This year, much of the world’s attention turned decisively towards Artificial Intelligence. Few technologies in recent memory have generated such widespread interest, debate and investment. While every generation believes it is witnessing extraordinary change, there are moments when technology genuinely alters the trajectory of industries and societies. Like the Internet and mobile computing before it, I believe AI represents one such moment.
As new technologies emerge, the most important differentiator will not simply be access to tools, but the ability to use them to solve real business problems. Technology will change many things, but judgement, creativity and integrity will still matter deeply.
At the same time, organisations are being required to confront important questions around privacy, security, governance and data sovereignty. These considerations cannot be treated as afterthoughts. The future will require enterprises to balance innovation with trust,

I remain optimistic about the future. Not because change can be predicted with certainty, but because adaptability, learning and disciplined execution have always been part of Persistent’s foundation. Technology will continue to evolve. Markets will continue to change. New opportunities and new challenges will emerge. What gives me confidence is the quality of our people, the trust of our customers and the values that have guided us for more than three decades. These strengths have carried us through previous transitions, and I believe they will continue to serve us well in the years ahead.

For Persistent, this transition aligns closely with our heritage and our strengths. For more than thirty-five years, we have helped customers navigate major technology transitions by combining deep engineering expertise with a strong understanding of enterprise systems and data. Throughout this period, our work has focused on helping customers build, modernise and manage the technology foundations that support their businesses. As enterprises move from automation towards intelligence, these foundations become even more important.
Finally, I would like to thank our customers, partners, vendors and communities for the role each continues to play in the company we are building together. In the end, companies are built by people, relationships and shared beliefs sustained over many years. We have been fortunate in all three.
Our growth continued with consistency in FY26, marking our 24th consecutive quarter of growth. This achievement reflects the trust of our customers, the strength of our strategy and the commitment of our people. I thank every employee for the professionalism, resilience and care they bring to their work each day. I would also like to acknowledge the support of their families, whose encouragement and understanding make these achievements possible in countless ways.

Dear Shareholders,

Dear Shareholders,
FY26 marked a defining year in the evolution of enterprise AI. Across industries, the conversation shifted decisively from experimentation to execution. Organisations are no longer asking what AI can do; they are asking how quickly and effectively it can be embedded into products, processes, decisions and customer experiences.
announce a final dividend of INR 18 per share, bringing the total dividend for the year to INR 40 per share. These results reflect the growing demand for AI-led modernisation, the dedication of our teams and the trust our clients continue to place in Persistent.
Through our work with enterprises around the world, we have learned that successful AI adoption depends on three critical capabilities: a strong technology foundation, deep business context and the ability to embed intelligence into workflows where decisions and outcomes are created. We describe this through our 3C Framework — Core, Context and Coordination. Together, these capabilities help enterprises move beyond pilots and translate AI investments into measurable business value.

Throughout my career, I have witnessed several technology transitions reshape our industry, from distributed computing and the internet to cloud and digital transformation. What makes AI different is its ability to influence not only technology architectures, but also how organisations operate, make decisions and create value. The next competitive advantage will come from how effectively intelligence is integrated into the operating core of the enterprise.
Message from the CEO
This represents a significant opportunity for Persistent. Organisations increasingly need partners that can combine AI capabilities with engineering rigour and accountable execution. Our heritage in product engineering, combined with deep expertise in enterprise modernisation, positions us uniquely to help clients operationalise intelligence across their technology landscape, data estate and business operations.
At Persistent, we believe this is where our engineering heritage creates a distinct advantage. Our roots in software and product engineering have shaped our approach to technology innovation for more than three decades. As enterprises seek to operationalise AI, the combination of product engineering excellence, data expertise, domain knowledge and disciplined execution is becoming increasingly important.

The next phase of enterprise transformation will be defined not by access to AI, but by the ability to operationalise it responsibly, at scale and with measurable business impact.
Our AI-led, platform-driven services strategy continues to strengthen this differentiation. By combining software engineering, cloud, data, platforms and AI, we help clients modernise core systems, accelerate innovation and build more intelligent enterprises.
Our performance in FY26 reflects the strength of this positioning. Revenue reached $1.654 billion, growing 17.4% year-over-year, while Q4 marked our 24th consecutive quarter of revenue growth. We are also pleased to

Looking ahead, I believe AI will be one of the most powerful drivers of productivity, innovation and economic value creation over the coming decade. Organisations that successfully combine technology, data, talent and governance will be best positioned to capture its full potential.
A defining moment of the year was our recognition as a Microsoft Frontier Firm for leadership in Agentic AI. Persistent enters this next chapter with confidence. Our product engineering DNA, AI-led, platform-driven services strategy, ecosystem partnerships and global talent base position us uniquely to help clients navigate this transformation and create enduring value for all stakeholders.

MyLife @Persistent

MyLife @Persistent
At Persistent, well-being is not a benefit, it is a belief. Created by Dr. Anand Deshpande,
MyLife@Persistent continues to be the cultural and structural backbone of how we care for our
people. In FY26, the framework evolved from a wellness programme to a holistic charter, to help
employees and their families lead healthier, more connected and more fulfilling lives.
Rooted in our philosophy of work-life harmony, MyLife@Persistent operates across the four
dimensions of Physical, Emotional, Social and Financial Wellness, delivered through the eight
structured offerings of Awareness & Education, Workshops, Communities, Transformation
Programmes, Personalised Counselling, Flagship Events, Unwind & Energisers and Team Bonding.
In FY26, we deepened personalisation further through our N=1 approach, scaled the wellness
ambassadors programme across global locations and introduced gamified digital challenges that
made everyday well-being more engaging.
The result: a vibrant ecosystem where every employee feels seen, supported and celebrated.

Dear Stakeholders,
Governance remains central to our approach. We strengthened oversight through a double materiality assessment integrated into our Enterprise Risk Management framework and established a value-chain reporting process aligned with SEBI's BRSR requirements. As AI adoption accelerates, we believe responsible innovation must remain closely tied to transparency, ethics and human impact.

At Persistent, ESG is not a parallel agenda but a core enabler of long-term resilience, responsible growth and stakeholder trust. As technology reshapes industries and societies, we believe enterprises that combine innovation with accountability and growth with stewardship will define responsible leadership in the AI era, resulting in strengthened operational resilience, responsible decision-making and enduring trust with clients, partners, investors and communities.
On the social front, we achieved 98% overall learning coverage through continuous learning and AI-led skilling, trained 75% of suppliers (by value) on ESG aspects and 99.43% of employees completed training on EHS, Human Rights and the Annual Policy Compliance - Code of Conduct. Our improved Carbon Disclosure Project score from B to A places us among the top 4% of companies globally. With our inclusion in the Dow Jones Best-in-Class World Index and a CSA score of 86, we now rank among the top 10% of IT services companies in the S&P Global Sustainability Yearbook 2026.
As a UN Global Compact participant, with Net Zero 2050 targets approved by the Science Based Targets initiative (SBTi), we remain aligned with globally recognised frameworks and climate science.

As a UN Global Compact participant, with Net Zero 2050 targets approved by the Science Based Targets initiative (SBTi), we remain aligned with globally recognised frameworks and climate science.
During FY26, we translated ESG commitments into measurable progress. We achieved a 62.90% reduction in market- based emissions and a 20.20% reduction in location-based emissions across Scope 1, 2 and 3 (from the FY24 baseline), while sustaining carbon neutrality for Scope 1 and Scope 2 emissions for the third year in a row. Global renewable energy adoption rose from 56.83% to 68.22%, with India-owned locations reaching 96.54%. We achieved Zero Waste to Landfill (ZWL) certification for six India-owned operations, along with 100% wastewater recycling, an 11.01% reduction in freshwater consumption, and plantation of nearly two lakh trees through Persistent Foundation initiatives.
Environmental, Social and Governance
Looking ahead, we remain focused on deepening ESG integration across strategy, operations and value chains, balancing innovation, governance and societal impact to build durable long-term value.
As AI adoption accelerates, we believe responsible innovation must remain closely tied to transparency, ethics and human impact.

As Joey Tribbiani of the famous show Friends says, “A selfless good deed does not exist,” because doing good makes you feel good. Psychologists and philosophers have believed that every action, however altruistic, is always motivated by the desire to feel happy. I endorse this theory through lived experience. The emotions of gratification, joy, contentment and humility that I feel at the beginning and end of each year add to my repertoire of life’s memories of serving the society.

The Persistent Foundation is 17 years old. We have been in the business of giving back to society and making a difference for close to two decades. The impact created in the neighbourhoods we work with has been tangible and perceptible. The different communities we have served, including school students, women, farmers, infants, girls in college, senior citizens, the specially abled, the mentally ill, rural communities, animals and birds, have benefitted from various interventions such as education scholarships, health screenings, cataract surgeries, cleft surgeries, cochlear implants, vaccinations, afforestation, building wells and dams, cattle breeding, fodder and vaccinations, conserving rare bird species, building an aviary, helping in tiger census exercises, monitoring elephant movement and several other initiatives.

The Foundation executed several key projects for Community Development. Providing better farming techniques, better quality seeds and fertilisers, training in artificial intelligence and its uses in agricultural practices, efficient irrigation cycles, building dams and bunds to store water, and desalting of streams and canals are some of the initiatives undertaken in rural communities. We planted more than 40,000 trees this year across seven locations, enabling afforestation and helping restore forest cover. We helped install 350 domestic biogas plants in homes across more than 100 villages, providing a sustainable alternative to cooking gas. This initiative was so well received that villagers contributed to the cost themselves. The construction of wells to provide easy access to drinking water has earned us countless blessings. Solar lifts and pumps help irrigate farms. Building reservoirs to store water helps farming communities harvest one additional crop, increasing both yield and income. All of these interventions have contributed to improving agricultural productivity and livelihoods.

Our CSR initiatives in the US have been gathering momentum during the past year. We have taken baby steps towards serving local communities there. We were saddened to observe homelessness and hunger within affluent cities. The World Food Movement helped us provide hot meals to underprivileged students, homeless adults and homeless veterans in New York. Elijah’s Promise did the same in New Jersey, as did Sai Ashraya in Santa Clara. The Shakti campaign was launched to help destitute women re-enter the job market and become financially independent. School kits and hygiene kits were assembled and distributed to local schools and veteran organisations. The wheels have been put in motion across seven locations in the US, and positive energy flows in from all directions. Our enthusiastic employees in Dallas and Seattle have also engaged with local schools and veteran communities to provide support for their initiatives. The most thrilling moment for us was participating in the Veterans Day Parade in New York on November 11, commemorating 250 years of the US Military. Fifteen employees from the Bridgewater office in New Jersey walked in the parade, and it was a proud moment for us to be part of such a historic event.

At Persistent Foundation, we believe meaningful progress is created when
innovation, inclusion and collective action come together with a purpose.
As technology reshapes industries and societies at unprecedented speed,
we believe it must also expand opportunity, strengthen resilience and contribute
meaningfully to the communities and ecosystems that sustain long-term progress.
For more than 17 years, the Foundation has worked alongside marginalised and
underprivileged communities, institutions and grassroots partners to help create
opportunities that endure beyond individual interventions. Whether through
education, healthcare, environmental stewardship or livelihood creation, our focus
remains on enabling long-term capability, dignity and self-reliance. Increasingly,
we see this work not only as social responsibility, but as part of building a more
inclusive and resilient future in which progress is shared more widely and sustainably.

impact, delivering 65 projects across Education, Health, Community Development
and the Preservation of Heritage and Wildlife. Together, these initiatives touched
the lives of 70,000 individuals and 600 families. We also enabled the plantation of

objective is to move beyond short-term intervention towards enabling durable
capability and opportunity that can sustain and compound over time.

FY 2025-26 reflects Persistent’s continued commitment to financial discipline, operational excellence, and sustainable value creation. Despite a dynamic macroeconomic environment characterised by geopolitical uncertainties, currency fluctuations, and evolving market conditions, we remained focused on executing our strategic priorities, investing prudently, and driving operational efficiencies. These efforts enabled us to deliver strong financial performance while further strengthening our balance sheet.
Strengthening Performance Through Operational Excellence
At Persistent, our culture of financial discipline is underpinned by a relentless focus on productivity and efficiency. During the year, we accelerated the adoption of AI, automation, and digitalisation across our operations, enabling greater scalability and improved cost management.
Navigating Uncertainty with Discipline

Navigating Uncertainty with Discipline
The technology industry continued to operate amid heightened uncertainty during the year, shaped by geopolitical tensions, including the conflict in the Middle East, supply chain disruptions, currency volatility, and the rapid emergence of AI-led disruption across the technology landscape. As enterprises reassessed investment priorities and accelerated the adoption of AI-powered solutions, the industry experienced significant shifts in demand patterns, operating models, and competitive dynamics.
We also enhanced utilisation levels and implemented targeted pricing initiatives, which contributed to improved operating leverage. Additionally, the depreciation of the Indian rupee provided a favourable tailwind. Together, these factors strengthened our profitability profile and supported margin expansion.
Message from the CFO
As a result, we delivered an EBIT margin of 15.6%, despite absorbing a one-time impact of 0.6% related to the New Labour Code. This performance remains aligned with our long- term objective of maintaining EBIT margins in the 16%–17% range.

Delivering Strong Financial Results

Report of the Directors
Your Directors are pleased to present the Thirty-sixth Annual Report of your Company along with the Audited Financial Statements for the Financial Year ended March 31, 2026.
A. Business Update
The theme of this year’s report, Re(AI)magining the Enterprise, reflects both the moment our industry has reached and the role your Company has chosen within it. Across the world, enterprises are rethinking how they operate, transform, and compete in the presence of Artificial Intelligence. Ambition is everywhere; what remains scarce is the engineering execution to turn that ambition into something impactful, governed, and measurable. That intersection, where AI ambition meets engineering execution, is where your Company does its most consequential work.

It is also where Persistent has always operated. For thirty-six years, your Company has been built not around any single technology wave but around a more enduring belief that a company stays valuable by continuing to learn, adapt, and earn its customers’ trust through every cycle of change. AI is the latest and most far-reaching of those cycles, and one that rewards precisely the strengths your Company has spent decades cultivating, which include engineering judgement, technical depth, and the discipline to execute responsibly at scale.

Your Company entered this moment having built capability ahead of demand, and Financial Year 2025-26 reflected the payoff. In Financial Year 2025-26, Revenue was US$ 1,654.4 Million, growing 17.4% Year-on-Year in US$ terms and 23.5% in Indian Rupee terms, strengthening your Company’s standing among the fastest-growing companies in the industry. Q4FY 26 marked the 24th consecutive quarter of sequential growth; a cadence achieved by only a handful of companies. Profitability strengthened even as the Company continued to invest ahead of demand, full-year EBIT margin expanded to 15.6%, and Profit After Tax rose 33% to INR 18,651 Million, with the fourth-quarter EBIT margin reaching 16.3%. On the strength of this performance, the Board recommended a final dividend of INR 18 per share, bringing the total dividend for the year to INR 40 per share, up from INR 35 per share a year earlier, subject to shareowners’ approval. As AI adoption accelerated, your Company’s AI-led, platform-driven approach strengthened its operating model from within, improving the quality, velocity, and scale of everything it delivers. The defining lesson of the year, visible across every industry, is that success with AI depends less on the sophistication of any single model than on operational maturity, including clean, well-governed data, redesigned processes, an enabled workforce, and responsible governance. Enterprises are no longer seeking a vendor of AI features; they are seeking a partner who can make AI work safely, repeatably, and accountably, inside the systems on which their business already runs. That is the role your Company has built itself to play: through a model that is platform-centric, IP-led, and outcome-based, and in which it is consistently its own first customer.

Across its three industry verticals, Software, Hi-Tech and Emerging Industries; Banking, Financial Services and Insurance; and Healthcare and Life Sciences, this strategy is advancing on several reinforcing fronts:
• Engineering Hyper Productivity. Your Company’s Generative AI-enabled engineering platform, SASVA, reached its fourth generation, with SASVA 4.0 becoming generally available in April 2026 and backed by a portfolio of more than 120 patents. Shifting the focus from individual productivity to team intelligence, its “Brain” holds the full organisational context and validates workflows by simulation before execution, while integration with partner models, frontier models such as Anthropic’s Claude and OpenAI’s GPT, lets clients bring their own model of choice and tooling into a single, governed environment that accelerates software development and reduces technical debt at scale.
• Business Hyper Productivity. Your Company is reimagining end-to-end business workflows as self-orchestrating ecosystems of AI agents. During the year it enhanced its GenAI Hub and Agent Studio, launched an Agent Processing Unit to onboard and orchestrate external agents, and grew its portfolio to more than 250 enterprise agents with deep domain coverage across BFSI and Healthcare and Life Sciences.

• Enterprise Data Readiness. Trusted, contextual and governed data is the foundation of scaled enterprise AI readiness and adoption. To accelerate this journey, your Company enhanced its iAURA platform with a modern interface, agentified Data Engineering Lifecycle, and an AI Data Mapper and Modeller grounded in a semantic layer. A new Enterprise Data Assessment capability builds knowledge graphs and enterprise data context, capturing business meaning, relationships, and domain knowledge, giving AI agents the memory to act with precision. A Cost of Intelligence capability brings governance, making AI spend measurable and accountable, giving enterprises the trusted foundations on which durable AI value is built.

• Customer Zero. Your Company is its own first customer, deploying its modular Agentic AI platform, AssistX, across its internal functions to compress incident-resolution times and automate large parts of its operations, moving from systems of record to systems of action. Every capability therefore reaches clients already proven in production, and the experience continually sharpens the Company’s offerings.

• Non-linear, platform-led economics. Platform-driven pricing is contributing a meaningful margin tailwind, as your Company progressively shifts its revenue mix towards non-linear engagements in which value is increasingly decoupled from headcount.
• Vertical depth. Representative engagements during the year included a large-scale shift from hardware-centric products to software-led platforms for a global industrial technology leader, the modernisation of a payments platform for one of the largest banks in the Nordics, the co-building of a fully digital underwriting platform for one of Australia’s largest life insurers, and the reimagining of a global Contract Research Organisation platform into a single, cloud-first architecture for a global life sciences leader.
Underpinning these engagements is your Company’s 3C Framework, Core, Context, and Coordination. This architecture enables enterprises to move AI from fragmented pilots to integrated, enterprise-wide results.
Core provides the governed, cloud-agnostic foundation that secures, observes, and cost-controls every AI workload from day one.
Context supplies the enterprise intelligence, grounding agents in verified data, knowledge graphs, institutional memory, and domain semantics so that they speak the language of the business.

Context supplies the enterprise intelligence, grounding agents in verified data, knowledge graphs, institutional memory, and domain semantics so that they speak the language of the business.
Coordination orchestrates auditable, multi-agent workflows across functions and systems of record, enabling people and agents to collaborate at production scale with full traceability. Each pillar reinforces the others, and together they turn isolated AI experiments into outcomes the business can trust and repeat — the foundation on which your Company is building durable, AI-led transformation for its clients.

Your Company continued to widen the ecosystem through which it builds the next generation of solutions. During the year, NVIDIA elevated your company to its Advanced Technology Partner program and partnered on a drug-discovery accelerator; AWS enhanced your company’s partnership status to Strategic Global Systems Integrator; Microsoft awarded the final designations needed to complete all six Solution Partner Designations; and ServiceNow elevated your company to Premier partner. Your Company also deepened its partnerships and innovations with Databricks and Snowflake, advanced model-development collaborations with Anthropic and OpenAI, and announced a new partnership with Lyzr AI for enterprise process modernisation. Your Company also deepened its collaboration with academia, co-developing the AI Value Compass with IIM Ahmedabad, a research-based framework for prioritising and scaling enterprise AI investments. This partnership is part of a broader commitment to co-innovate with leading institutions and help elevate the country’s AI talent landscape.

To enable and empower every team member of your Company across 21 countries, along this AI transformation journey, your Company convened AI Huddle in Pune for more than 1700 senior leaders and engineers and, through Persistent University and a company-wide AI fluency program, completed over 32,500 internal and 6,000 external AI certifications during the year.
Your Company’s momentum was widely recognised worldwide. It was named the fastest-growing IT services brand globally in the 2026 Brand Finance IT Services 25 Report, ranked among Asia-Pacific’s top 10 Professional Services Companies in the TIME 2026 list, and positioned as a Leader in both the Everest Group Software Product Engineering and Private Equity Services PEAK Matrix® Assessments 2026. It was named a Strong Performer in the Gartner Voice of the Customer for Public Cloud IT Transformation Services 2026, and its talent and people practices were honoured at the ET Human Capital Awards, the InfiniT Awards, and by the Confederation of Indian Industry.

Your Company’s commitment to responsible business deepened further. Its sustainability performance earned best- in-class ratings, including continued recognition in the Dow Jones Sustainability Indices and an S&P Global Corporate Sustainability Assessment score of 86. Your Company also continued to make progress on renewable energy across its owned campuses and to scale community and life-saving initiatives through the Persistent Foundation across India and the United States. Through it all, your Company holds to a human-centred view of this technology: AI does not replace people; it enables them to do far more, far faster, and judgment, creativity, and integrity will matter more, not less, in the years ahead.

Policy for the appointment of a new director on the Board
The Board of Directors decides the criteria for the appointment of a new director on the Board from time to time depending on the dates of retirement of existing Directors and the strategic needs of your Company. For every new member to be added, at least three members of the NRC interact with the panel of candidates. The panel consists of at least two to four potential candidates.
Efforts are made to ensure that the Board has adequate diversity across various parameters such as nationality, expertise and gender in terms of the Board Diversity Policy. ‘Saksham Niveshak’ Campaign initiated by the Investor Education and Protection Fund Authority (IEPFA)
IEPFA, under the Ministry of Corporate Affairs (MCA), launched the 100 Day Campaign titled ‘Saksham Niveshak’ vide circular dated July 16, 2025, and the campaign was conducted during the period July 28, 2025 to November 6, 2025. The objective of the campaign was to assist shareholders in claiming their unpaid or unclaimed dividends and updating KYC details in order to prevent transfer of such dividends and corresponding shares to the Investor Education and Protection Fund (IEPF).

In line with the IEPFA’s directives and as part of its continued focus on proactive shareholder engagement, your Company implemented the First 100 Day ‘Saksham Niveshak’ Campaign covering shareholders with unpaid or unclaimed dividends from FY 2017-18 to FY 2024-25. The Company issued formal communications and a public notice to apprise shareholders of the campaign and encouraged timely updating of KYC details to facilitate dividend claims. Relevant campaign information and notices were made available on the Company’s website to ensure ease of access. Further, the Company worked closely with its Registrar and Share Transfer Agent to support shareholders in resolving queries and updating records, with the objective of enabling seamless dividend credit and minimising transfers to the IEPF.

IEPFA, Ministry of Corporate Affairs, Government of India, vide its communication dated March 27, 2026, has initiated the second 100 Day Campaign for the period from April 1, 2026, to July 9, 2026. In alignment with the objectives of the IEPFA, your Company is extending its full support to this initiative by encouraging Members to complete the requisite KYC formalities with the Registrar and Share Transfer Agent/Depository Participants and claim their rightful dividend amounts within the stipulated timeline.
The Board has appointed Mr. Amit Atre, Company Secretary, as the Nodal Officer under this campaign to ensure compliance with the IEPF rules. His coordinates form part of the Report on Corporate Governance in this Annual Report.

The Board of Directors of your Company has developed a Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) Policy to serve as a framework for guiding the Company’s CSR initiatives. This policy is publicly accessible and can be viewed on the Company’s official website at CSR Policy.pdf
The CSR Policy outlines the belief that as a responsible Company, employing a large number of employees, it is the Company’s obligation to contribute to society and the community. The Company has held this belief since inception. The journey began in 1995 when the Board decided to commit 1% of profits for social causes. The allocation was subsequently increased to 2% following the introduction of the CSR provisions under the Companies Act, 2013.

Wildlife and Heritage conservation — Rooting advancement in our cultural and natural inheritance
As part of its commitment to protecting wildlife and maintaining ecological balance, the Foundation supported the use of technology to strengthen conservation efforts and reduce conflict between humans and wildlife. Drone cameras were deployed to track the movement of wild animals and monitor forest areas. These drones were also used for tiger census activities and to observe elephant movement in sensitive corridors. This enabled timely monitoring, better coordination on the ground, and quicker response to potential risks.
These efforts support the forest department in safeguarding wildlife habitats and help create awareness among local

These efforts support the forest department in safeguarding wildlife habitats and help create awareness among local
communities. By providing early alerts and reliable tracking information, the initiatives play an important role in preventing
human-wildlife conflict and improving safety for both people and animals.
Alongside wildlife conservation, the Foundation also supported heritage preservation and public education by contributing to
the upkeep and improvement of museum infrastructure. This included maintenance work and upgrades to essential facilities,
enabling effective use of audio guide systems for visitors.
Infrastructure support was also extended to Shivsrushti, a historic theme park in Pune, where digital display screens were
installed to enhance storytelling and provide visitors with a more engaging and educational experience through immersive
visual content.
In line with its CSR commitment to wildlife care, the Foundation also supported the operations of an aviary providing medical
treatment to injured and rescued birds. During the year, 673 birds across six species received care, of which 509 were
successfully rehabilitated and released back into their natural habitats. These efforts contributed meaningfully to biodiversity
conservation and the restoration of local ecosystems.

Employee Engagement
At the Foundation, employee engagement is at the heart of its CSR efforts, reflecting a culture where employees voluntarily contribute their time, skills, and care to support communities. Through well-structured volunteering opportunities across education, health, environment, and community development, employees are encouraged to participate actively and create meaningful social impact.
During the year, employee volunteering continued to see strong participation. A total of 5,841 employees contributed 11,683 hours across 70 initiatives. Overall, 299 volunteering activities were conducted across 15 locations, reflecting broad participation and geographic reach.
Volunteering programmes were designed to be inclusive and flexible, enabling employees across roles and locations to participate alongside their regular work commitments. On average, each volunteer contributed close to two hours, reflecting consistent and high quality engagement. Locations such as Pune, Nagpur, Hyderabad, and Goa recorded particularly strong participation, supported by effective local coordination and employee-led initiatives.

In addition to volunteering, employees actively supported the Foundation through donation drives, further strengthening the culture of giving. Employee contributions during the year amounted to INR 47.12 lakh, supplemented by INR 34.79 lakh from other sources. Together, these contributions played an important role in strengthening the Foundation’s social programmes and extending their reach.

Company’s beliefs on Corporate Governance
“Corporate governance is concerned with holding the balance between economic and social goals and aligning the interests of individuals, corporations and society.” - Sir Adrian Cadbury
Redefining Stakeholders for a Sustainable Future
Traditionally, the stakeholders of a public limited company have been defined in legal terms, comprising shareholders, debenture-holders, deposit-holders, and other security holders. While such a definition remains relevant, the Company believes that in the context of a modern and evolving business environment, the scope of stakeholders must extend far beyond statutory classifications.
At Persistent, we recognise that long-term value creation is intrinsically linked with the interests of all those who contribute to, and are impacted by, our operations. Accordingly, our approach to stakeholder engagement encompasses not only our investors, but also our employees and their families, customers, business partners, vendors, regulators, and the communities and ecosystems within which we operate.

In line with this philosophy, the Board of Directors has affirmed a broader and more inclusive definition of stakeholders. This approach aligns with the Company’s sustainability vision and reinforces its commitment to creating shared and enduring value for all stakeholder groups.
Our Commitment to Responsible Governance
Corporate Governance is a fundamental cornerstone of our operations and is anchored in the principles of trust, transparency, and accountability. Our governance framework is designed to balance the interests of a diverse stakeholder base while enabling robust and ethical decision-making that supports sustainable business growth.
Integrity, inclusivity, and sustainability are fundamental to the Company’s corporate culture. Through continuous enhancement of governance practices, we strive to uphold the highest standards of accountability while contributing positively to the broader economic, social, and environmental ecosystem.
This section presents an overview of how the Company engages with stakeholders, integrates Environmental, Social, and Governance (ESG) considerations into strategy, and seeks to deliver long-term sustainable value.
1. Employees and their Families

1. Employees and their Families
The Company’s continued success is driven by the expertise, commitment, and dedication of employees. Senior employees play a critical role in shaping the Company’s strategic direction and overseeing operations. Recognising the vital support extended by employees’ families, the Company remains committed to safeguarding their overall well-being.
2. Clients
The Company provides services to its clients because of which we earn our revenue. Their satisfaction and delight are important focus areas of the Company’s operations. Our clients are keen that we succeed and continue to deliver on our promises and hence, they are also vested in our success.
3. Partners
The Company collaborates with its partners to deliver value to its clients. These relationships are built on mutual trust and shared objectives. The Company believes that the strength and success of its partnerships are integral to its own growth and endeavours to support the long-term success of its partners.
4. Suppliers
The Company relies on a network of suppliers for various goods and services essential to its operations. Operational efficiency is closely linked to the quality and reliability of these contributions. The Company is committed to maintaining fair and sustainable relationships with its suppliers and supporting their long-term growth.

Shareowners are the owners of the Company and are the traditional stakeholders in the Company. They have
invested in the Company, and we believe it is our responsibility to deliver fair returns to our shareowners.
6. Environment
It is a constant endeavour of the Company to conserve and preserve the environment. Over the years, the Company
has focused on sustainable business practices encompassing economic, environmental, and social imperatives. The
Company also works through Persistent Foundation and Persistent India Foundation, to support projects in the areas of
environmental sustainability and ecological balance.

The Company believes that strong Corporate Governance practices are essential for enhancing long-term stakeholder

strengthen resilience, and support sustainable growth.

The Board reviewed and discussed the outcomes of the evaluation in an executive session and noted that the Board, its Committees and the Directors, including the Independent Directors, continued to function effectively and demonstrated a high level of engagement, objectivity and preparedness in their roles. The evaluation process also enabled identification of areas for continuous improvement further improving overall Board effectiveness. The Board has taken note of these inputs and will address them as part of its ongoing governance and development initiatives.

Code of Conduct
Pursuant to the requirements of Regulation 17(5)(a) of Listing Regulations, the Company obtains the affirmation of compliance of the Code of Conduct from its Directors and Senior Management on a yearly basis since Financial Year 2005-06. Furthermore, the Code of Conduct applies to all the Company employees and its subsidiaries.
The Code of Conduct is an annual declaration that helps remind all employees and stakeholders the importance of maintaining the highest standards of ethical business conduct for the Company. In terms of the Code of Conduct, Directors and Employees must act within the guidelines of the authority conferred upon them and with a duty to make and enact informed decisions and policies in the best interests of the Company and its shareholders and stakeholders.

Further, Directors and Employees must ensure that they do not derive any undue personal benefit due to their position in the Company and from the access they have to certain confidential information coming to their knowledge.
It has been affirmed by the Board of Directors that the Code of Conduct has been complied with by all the Board members and all the Employees and a declaration to this effect forms part of this Report. The Code of Conduct is uploaded on the website of the Company at Code of Conduct for Directors and Employees | Persistent Systems
In addition to the annual Code of Conduct, the Board has also established a robust Code of Conduct on Prevention of Insider Trading in terms of the SEBI (Prohibition of Insider Trading) Regulations, 2015. The Company has a zero tolerance policy towards insider trading, corruption, bribery, and money laundering.

Board deliberations on strategy planning
As part of our annual strategy planning process, the Company organises sessions for the Board Members and Senior Executives to deliberate on various topics related to technological overview, global scenario for the IT industry, sales strategy, market research, risk overview, succession planning and strategic programs required to achieve the Company’s long-term objectives.

The Company organises periodic planning meetings called the ‘Huddle’, which is attended by all the senior sales and delivery leaders of the Organisation. Board Members participate in the Huddle to get a first-hand view of the strategy planning and implementation process and guide the leadership by offering their expertise.
This serves a dual purpose of providing a platform for Board Members to bring their expertise to the projects, while also providing an opportunity for them to understand detailed aspects of execution and challenges relating to the business of the Company.
Whistleblower Policy
The Board of Directors of the Company has a Whistleblower Policy for employees and non-employee stakeholders in India and all global locations. The employees are encouraged to report to the Whistleblower Administrator if they observe any fraudulent financial or other information or conduct that results in instances of unethical behaviour, or actual or suspected violations of the Company’s Code of Conduct and the Ethics Policy.

The employees are actively encouraged to reach out to the Whistleblower Administrator if they observe any fraudulent activity, questionable financial practices, or conduct that appears unethical, or if they suspect violations of the Company’s Code of Conduct or Ethics Policy. Beginning FY 2025-26, the Head of the Ethics Committee serves as the Whistleblower Administrator, personally overseeing the investigation process from the initial complaint through to its resolution. All findings and outcomes are subsequently reported to the Chairperson of the Audit Committee. Importantly, complainants are permitted to submit their concerns in any local language, ensuring accessibility for all.
The Company has also taken proactive initiatives to train employees and raise awareness about the Vigil Mechanism, reinforcing a culture of transparency and ethical conduct. These initiatives, along with the policy itself, provide robust safeguards to protect employees from any form of victimisation when they report issues to the Whistleblower Administrator.

Your Company’s development centres are certified under ISO 27001, ISO 27017, ISO 27018, ISO 27701, ISO 22301, ISO 42001 and SOC 2 Type II.

Your Company is focused on cyber resilience and provides all the necessary budgets needed to build a robust cyber resilience. Your Company’s cloud first strategy is enabled by cloud security measures spanning access management, cloud data security, ensuring privacy in the cloud, safeguarding cloud workloads, effective monitoring and incident management of the cloud aligned to business-relevant outcomes. Global Business Outlook
The global economy enters Financial Year 2025-26 against a backdrop of slowing growth and renewed inflationary pressure. These conditions are linked to last year’s trade barriers and elevated uncertainty, with ongoing conflict in the Middle East compounding the strain. The challenges are particularly acute for emerging markets and developing economies, which remain more vulnerable to external shocks and financial instability.
While increased defense spending in response to geopolitical tension may provide a temporary boost to economic activity, it also intensifies inflationary pressure and strains fiscal health, raising the likelihood of social unrest in fragile regions. The overall outlook remains clouded by substantial downside risks, including prolonged conflict, deepening geopolitical fragmentation and the resurgence of protectionist trade policies.

In this volatile environment, organisations are under pressure to strike a careful balance between cost efficiency and the need to build resilience, agility and progress toward climate objectives, especially as regulatory frameworks grow more complex and unpredictable. At the same time, rapid advances in automation and artificial intelligence are helping to reduce operational workloads, but these technologies require strong governance structures and proactive workforce reskilling to ensure successful integration. As your Company looks to 2026 and 2027, the pace of disruption is accelerating, with technology companies moving from experimental AI pilots to large-scale, ROI-focused deployments that prioritise safety, security and regulatory compliance, while also laying the groundwork for the adoption of transformative quantum technologies.
Company Outlook
Your Company is a premier global provider of digital engineering and enterprise modernisation services. With more than 27,500 employees across 21 countries, it specialises in AI-driven solutions and software product engineering for industries such as BFSI, Healthcare and Hi-Tech, with deep expertise in building software products from conception to deployment. Its focus is on embedding AI-driven solutions across platforms, helping enterprises move from technical debt to competitive differentiation through a platform mindset.

Your company’s strategic approach centers on AI readiness through modern technology and data stacks, enabling clients to become value creators. It modernises core platforms and embeds AI across operations, aligning modernisation with strategic priorities to accelerate product launches, improve cost-to-income ratios and build customer trust. Building the AI-led Enterprise

Building the AI-led Enterprise
For most enterprises, the question is no longer whether to adopt Generative AI, but where AI creates genuine value and where greater autonomy introduces risk. The market is shifting decisively from experimentation to disciplined, large-scale production. Generative AI is now firmly established from pilot to deployment, toward Agentic AI woven into core business processes. Yet realising AI’s full potential remains demanding. Integrating intelligence with existing enterprise systems is both complex and expensive and outcomes must be governed, secure and dependable at scale.

Your Company’s AI strategy is anchored on three reinforcing pillars, underpinned by Responsible AI. Engineering Hyper-Productivity embeds AI across the software development lifecycle, so engineering teams deliver faster, raise quality and do more with less. Business Hyper-Productivity applies AI to automate and optimise business process workflows and decision-making across enterprise functions, enabling organisations to drive efficiency and faster outcomes. Enterprise Data Readiness prepares the enterprise data foundation, with the right structure, governance and accessibility so AI can deliver accurate, contextual and trusted outcomes at scale. Together, these pillars define the path enterprises must take to realise the full value of AI. Success lies in the last mile, making AI-driven outcomes repeatable, transparent and governed at scale, so that the desired business outcome is sustained and trusted across the enterprise.

Management Discussion and Analysis
Each of these pillars is brought to life by purpose-built Persistent platforms: SASVA for Engineering Hyper- Productivity, GenAI Hub and Agent Studio for Business Hyper-Productivity, and iAURA for Enterprise Data Readiness. SASVA 4.0 advances enterprise AI engineering further still, enabling human teams and AI agents to collaborate within governed boundaries to raise the quality and predictability of outcomes. Together, these platforms mark a generational shift in how enterprises build, deploy and govern AI.
The 3C Framework of Persistent AI

The 3C Framework of Persistent AI
Underpinning these platforms and client engagements is your Company’s 3C Framework — Core, Context and Coordination — an architecture that moves AI from fragmented pilots to integrated, enterprise-wide outcomes, and provides a repeatable path from experimentation to production at scale.
Core establishes the governed, cloud-agnostic foundation that secures, observes and cost-controls every AI workload from day one.
Context supplies the enterprise intelligence grounding agents in verified data, knowledge graphs, institutional memory and domain semantics so that they speak the language of the business.
Coordination orchestrates auditable, multi-agent workflows across functions and systems of record, enabling people and agents to collaborate at production scale with full traceability.
Each pillar reinforces the others. Together, they convert isolated experiments into outcomes the business can trust and repeat. The foundation on which your Company is building durable, AI-led transformation for its clients.

As per the accounting principles laid down in Ind AS 109 – ‘Financial Instruments’ relating to cash flow hedges, derivative financial instruments which qualify for cash flow hedge accounting are fair valued at balance sheet date and the effective portion of the resultant loss / (gain) is debited / (credited) to the hedge reserve under other comprehensive income and the ineffective portion is recognised in the statement of profit and loss. Derivative financial instruments are carried as forward contract receivable when the fair value is positive and as forward contract payable when the fair value is negative.

Changes in the fair value of derivative instruments that do not qualify for hedge accounting are recognised in the statement of profit and loss as they arise. Hedge accounting is discontinued when the hedging instrument expires or is sold, or terminated, or exercised or no longer qualifies for hedge accounting. Any cumulative gain or loss on the hedging instrument recognised under other comprehensive income is transferred to the statement of profit and loss when the forecasted transaction occurs or affects profit or loss or when a hedged transaction is no longer expected to occur.
Accordingly, the Forward Cover Reserve (net of tax effects) as at March 31, 2026, stood at a debit balance of INR 1,676.01 Million as against a debit balance of INR 2.32 Million as at March 31, 2025. Report on Risk Management
Persistent’s Approach to Risk Management
Persistent has a robust Enterprise Risk Management (ERM) framework comprising a formal risk management policy,
defined processes, governance mechanisms, and ongoing awareness programmes. Our ERM function is focused on

defined processes, governance mechanisms, and ongoing awareness programmes. Our ERM function is focused on
strengthening and embedding a proactive risk management culture across the organisation.
The ERM function works closely with various organisational units and business leadership to facilitate the identification,
assessment, and management of risks. Oversight is provided by the Risk Management Committee (RMC) of the Board
of Directors, which was constituted on April 24, 2017, ahead of the regulatory requirement for such a committee.
ERM Objectives
The key objectives of Persistent’s ERM function are to:
• Promote an effective system to manage risks essential to support the Company’s growth strategy and business
objectives, while ensuring resilience despite changing business dynamic
• Improve institutional decision-making by providing senior management and the Board with timely and accurate
information, and proposing mitigation plans, enabling them to better comprehend the risks and opportunities at the
enterprise level and make informed decisions
• Ensure that the Company meets all legal, regulatory, and policy compliance obligations
• Establish a structured process to identify and assess risks that may impact the business continuity of the Company,
and define appropriate response and recovery plans

and define appropriate response and recovery plans
• Proactively identify potential risks and opportunities to prepare for future challenges and breakthroughs
• Strengthen the organisation’s ability to comprehend, manage, and control risk exposures, fostering a culture of
responsible risk‑taking
• Integrate risk and opportunity assessment into the Company’s periodic planning procedures, such as strategic
planning and the annual budgeting cycle
• Promote a Risk‑Intelligent Culture wherein conscious, enterprise‑wide efforts are made to align the organisation’s
approach to risk, enabling consistent, risk-factored decision‑making through targeted programmes such as Risk
Familiarisation Programmes for Directors and Key Managerial Personnel, and risk training across key functions
ERM Framework
The Enterprise Risk Management (ERM) framework adopted by Persistent is aligned with ISO Standard 31000:2018
Risk Management — Guidelines, COSO ERM — Integrating Strategy and Performance (2017), and applicable
regulatory requirements in India. The framework takes a holistic approach to identifying the full range of risks the
Company faces, with particular emphasis on those that are critical to strategic success. The framework provides
guidance on identifying, assessing, measuring, monitoring, and responding to risks across the enterprise in alignment

guidance on identifying, assessing, measuring, monitoring, and responding to risks across the enterprise in alignment
with the Company’s objectives and risk appetite. The ERM function reports enterprise‑level risks to executive
leadership and the Risk Management Committee (RMC) of the Board on a timely basis as needed. A formal review is
conducted quarterly.
The Company’s risk management framework is further strengthened through the active involvement of internal auditors
and statutory auditors, who periodically review risk mitigation plans and related controls. Through their independent
assessments and audit processes, they provide oversight of the Company’s risk management practices — reinforcing
governance and supporting continuous improvement of enterprise risk management. The auditors also provide inputs
on key risk areas and emerging concerns as part of the overall risk management process.
Responsibility for managing risks is shared across the organisation to ensure an effective and consistent process
for avoiding and responding to risks in a timely manner. Dedicated leadership forums support the identification,
monitoring, and tracking of enterprise‑level risks, while the Risk Management Committee (RMC) of the Board has
ultimate oversight of the Company’s risk management function.

ERM Process Flow

ERM Process Flow
The risk management process followed at Persistent comprises the following key steps:
• Risk Identification: Identify plausible uncertainties and risks that may impact the achievement of functional, organisational,
and business objectives, or pose a threat to business continuity. This includes risks arising from internal operations as well as
external factors. Identified risks are categorised into financial, operational, reputational, regulatory, extended enterprise, strategic,
sustainability, talent, and technology for further assessment.
• Risk Analysis:
• Existing and newly identified risks are analysed based on impact, likelihood, and velocity and are evaluated against
established risk criteria, including potential business and financial impact
• For each enterprise‑level risk, Key Risk Indicators (KRIs) are defined and monitored against approved risk appetite and
tolerance thresholds to assess current risk health and the organisation’s readiness to manage it
• Where applicable, risks are assessed for potential financial exposure by identifying associated revenue, cost, or
operational drivers. Probability of occurrence, inferred from KRI performance and risk assessment, is applied to
estimate realistic downside impact and support prioritisation

estimate realistic downside impact and support prioritisation
• Selected risks are further analysed through scenario based assessments to evaluate the impact of plausible future
conditions such as regulatory changes, market movements, or technological developments. Scenario outcomes help
identify vulnerabilities and interdependencies, and inform mitigation planning
• Risk Prioritisation: Risks are prioritised based on criticality, emerging trends, and alignment with the Company’s objectives,
enabling focused management attention on key risks
• Risk Response: Appropriate risk response strategies are defined to avoid, mitigate, or manage key enterprise-level risks.
Mitigation plans are aligned to identified risk drivers, control effectiveness, and defined tolerance thresholds
• Monitor and Review: Mitigation actions are integrated into day‑to‑day operations and monitored through defined indicators.
The overall risk environment, effectiveness of mitigation measures, and emerging signals are reviewed periodically
• Reporting: Consolidated risk insights, including risk status and key trends, are reported to executive leadership and the Risk
Management Committee (RMC) of the Board on quarterly basis to support risk‑informed decision‑making and oversight

Reputational Risk of potential damage to reputation or loss of stakeholder confidence arising from non-compliance with risk management requirements, operational breakdown, legal or regulatory breach, unsuccessful product launches, or other adverse events
Regulatory Risk of potential fines, litigation costs, or enforcement actions from changes in the legal and regulatory environment, perceived or actual conflicts of interest, and potential actions or breaches of compliance and risk management requirements
Extended Enterprise Risk of potential disruption due to inadequate identification, assessment, or mitigation of risks associated with third‑party relationships
Sectoral Risks specific to the industry or sector in which the Company operates

Highlights of FY26

Highlights of FY26
FY2026 was marked by heightened geopolitical uncertainty and continued macro-economic volatility, including regional geopolitical developments, global trade and tariff-related uncertainty, and policy-led industry considerations. Throughout the year, the Company closely monitored these developments and activated appropriate mitigation measures to safeguard business continuity, workforce safety, and customer delivery. The Company’s diversified delivery footprint, established business continuity planning, and crisis management arrangements enabled stable operations during the period. These developments did not have a material impact on the Company’s operations, financial performance, or delivery commitments during FY 2026. However, given the evolving nature of the external risk environment, these areas remain under active monitoring and are supported by scenario-based contingency planning.
Geopolitical and macro-economic developments were assessed through structured enterprise-level risk reviews and ongoing management oversight. The Company’s service-oriented business model, geographic diversification, and limited exposure to high-risk regions supported operational resilience. Proactive stakeholder communication and operational flexibility further enabled continuity during the year.

Against this backdrop, the Company continued to strengthen its enterprise risk management framework with a forward-looking focus. Increased emphasis was placed on emerging and evolving risks, including artificial intelligence- related considerations, cyber security and data privacy, regulatory and labour-law developments, and macro-economic uncertainty. These risks were addressed through structured assessments, enhanced control frameworks, employee awareness initiatives, and scenario-based resilience testing to support informed decision-making.
Risk governance and crisis preparedness capabilities were further enhanced during the year. An integrated risk intelligence platform supported consolidated risk visibility, key risk indicator monitoring, and timely escalation to senior management and the Board Risk Committee. Ongoing regulatory monitoring, materiality reassessment, and strengthened governance practices reinforced the Company’s ability to anticipate and respond effectively to changes in the external risk environment.
The Company believes that the continued strengthening of risk governance, resilience, and forward-looking risk assessment capabilities remains critical to sustaining long-term growth and maintaining stakeholder confidence.

In view of the significance of the matter we applied the following audit procedures in this area, among others to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence:
The Group is required to test goodwill for impairment every year or more frequently when there is an indication of impairment. The impairment charge is determined by comparing the carrying value of goodwill with its recoverable amount. Recoverable amount is defined as the higher of value in use and fair value less cost of disposal. We consider the impairment testing of goodwill by the Group allocated to Cloud, Infrastructure and Security (CIS) and Customer Experience (CXCI) Cash Generating Units (CGUs) to involve significant estimates and judgment with a potential range of reasonable outcomes greater than our materiality for the consolidated financial statements as a whole.
• Obtained an understanding of Group’s evaluation of identification of cash generating units and allocation of goodwill to the respective CGUs.
• Obtained management’s assessment of recoverable amount and impairment assessment for goodwill.
• Tested the design, implementation and operating effectiveness of controls in respect of the Group’s impairment assessment process, including the periodic review of cashflow forecasts and valuation assumptions.

• Where management has used an independent valuer, evaluated the independent valuer’s competence, capabilities and objectivity, and assessing the valuation methodology used by the independent valuer to estimate the value in use.
There is inherent uncertainty involved in forecasting and discounting future cashflows, which are the basis of the assessment of recoverability. Considering the significant judgement involved, impairment of goodwill allocated to above mentioned CGUs are identified as key audit matter.

Opinion
In conjunction with our audit of the consolidated financial statements of Persistent Systems Limited (hereinafter referred to as “the Holding Company”) as of and for the year ended 31 March 2026, we have audited the internal financial controls with reference to financial statements of the Holding Company and such companies incorporated in India under the Act which are its subsidiary companies, as of that date.
In our opinion, the Holding Company and such companies incorporated in India which are its subsidiary companies, have, in all material respects, adequate internal financial controls with reference to financial statements and such internal financial controls were operating effectively as at 31 March 2026, based on the internal financial controls with reference to financial statements criteria established by such companies considering the essential components of such internal controls stated in the Guidance Note on Audit of Internal Financial Controls Over Financial Reporting issued by the Institute of Chartered Accountants of India (the “Guidance Note”).
Management’s and Board of Directors’ Responsibilities for Internal Financial Controls

Management’s and Board of Directors’ Responsibilities for Internal Financial Controls
The Holding Company’s Management and the Board of Directors are responsible for establishing and maintaining internal financial controls based on the internal financial controls with reference to financial statements criteria established by the Holding Company considering the essential components of internal control stated in the Guidance Note. These responsibilities include the design, implementation and maintenance of adequate internal financial controls that were operating effectively for ensuring the orderly and efficient conduct of its business, including adherence to the Holding Company’s policies, the safeguarding of its assets, the prevention and detection of frauds and errors, the accuracy and completeness of the accounting records, and the timely preparation of reliable financial information, as required under the Act.
Auditor’s Responsibility

Auditor’s Responsibility
Our responsibility is to express an opinion on the internal financial controls with reference to financial statements based on our audit. We conducted our audit in accordance with the Guidance Note and the Standards on Auditing, prescribed under Section 143(10) of the Act, to the extent applicable to an audit of internal financial controls with reference to financial statements. Those Standards and the Guidance Note require that we comply with ethical requirements and plan and perform the audit to obtain reasonable assurance about whether adequate internal financial controls with reference to financial statements were established and maintained and if such controls operated effectively in all material respects.

Our audit involves performing procedures to obtain audit evidence about the adequacy of the internal financial controls with reference to financial statements and their operating effectiveness. Our audit of internal financial controls with reference to financial statements included obtaining an understanding of internal financial controls with reference to financial statements, assessing the risk that a material weakness exists, and testing and evaluating the design and operating effectiveness of internal control based on the assessed risk. Meaning of Internal Financial Controls with Reference to Financial Statements

Meaning of Internal Financial Controls with Reference to Financial Statements
A company’s internal financial controls with reference to financial statements is a process designed to provide reasonable assurance regarding the reliability of financial reporting and the preparation of financial statements for external purposes in accordance with generally accepted accounting principles. A company’s internal financial controls with reference to financial statements include those policies and procedures that (1) pertain to the maintenance of records that, in reasonable detail, accurately and fairly reflect the transactions and dispositions of the assets of the company; (2) provide reasonable assurance that transactions are recorded as necessary to permit preparation of financial statements in accordance with generally accepted accounting principles, and that receipts and expenditures of the company are being made only in accordance with authorisations of management and directors of the company; and (3) provide reasonable assurance regarding prevention or timely detection of unauthorised acquisition, use, or disposition of the company’s assets that could have a material effect on the financial statements.
Inherent Limitations of Internal Financial Controls with Reference to Financial Statements

Inherent Limitations of Internal Financial Controls with Reference to Financial Statements
Because of the inherent limitations of internal financial controls with reference to financial statements, including the possibility of collusion or improper management override of controls, material misstatements due to error or fraud may occur and not be detected. Also, projections of any evaluation of the internal financial controls with reference to financial statements to future periods are subject to the risk that the internal financial controls with reference to financial statements may become inadequate because of changes in conditions, or that the degree of compliance with the policies or procedures may deteriorate.

Nature and purpose of reserves
a) General reserve

a) General reserve
The general reserve is a free reserve created by an appropriation from one component of equity (generally retained earnings) to another, not being an item of other comprehensive income (“OCI”). The same can be utilised in accordance with the provisions of the Companies Act, 2013.
b) Share options outstanding reserve
Share options outstanding reserve represents the cumulative expense recognised for equity-settled transactions at each reporting date until the employee share options are exercised / expired upon which such amount is transferred to General reserve.
c) Capital reserve
The excess of the Group’s portion of equity of the acquired company over its cost is treated as gain on bargain purchase and disclosed under Capital Reserve in the financial statements.
d) Capital redemption reserve
Capital redemption reserve represents the nominal value of the shares bought back; and is created and utilised in accordance with section 69 of the Companies Act, 2013.
e) Cash flow hedge reserve

e) Cash flow hedge reserve
When a derivative is designated as cashflow hedging instrument, the effective portion of changes in the fair value of derivative is recognised in other comprehensive income (OCI) and accumulated in cashflow hedge reserve. Cumulative gains or losses previously recognised in cashflow hedge reserve are recognised in the statement of profit and loss in the period in which such transaction occurs / hedging instruments are settled / cancelled.
f) Foreign currency translation reserve
The foreign exchange differences arising from the translation of financial statements of foreign operations with functional currency other than Indian rupees is recognised in other comprehensive income and is presented under equity in the foreign currency translation reserve. The amount is transferred to retained earnings upon disposal of investment in foreign operation.
g) PSPL ESOP Trust reserve and Treasury shares

g) PSPL ESOP Trust reserve and Treasury shares
The Group has created an Employee Stock Options Trust (ESOP Trust) for providing share-based payment to its employees. The Group uses ESOP Trust as a vehicle for distributing shares to employees. The ESOP Trust buys shares of the Company from the market, for giving shares to employees. The shares held by ESOP Trust are treated as treasury shares. Own equity instruments that are reacquired (treasury shares) are recognised at cost and deducted from equity. No gain or loss is recognised in profit or loss on the purchase, sale, issue or cancellation of the Group’s own equity instruments. Any difference between the carrying amount and the consideration, if reissued, is recognised in equity. Share options whenever exercised, would be satisfied with treasury shares.
h) Securities premium
Securities premium is used to record the premium on issue of shares. The reserve is utilised in accordance with the provisions of section 52 of the Companies Act, 2013.
i) Retained earnings
Retained earnings represent the amount of accumulated earnings of the Group which includes remeasurements of the defined benefit liabilities / asset.

3. Basis of consolidation
The consolidated financial statements of the Parent Company, its subsidiaries and the controlled trust (“the Group”) for the year ended March 31, 2025 are prepared in accordance with generally accepted accounting principles applicable in India, and the Indian Accounting Standard 110 (Ind AS 110) on ‘Consolidated Financial Statements’, notified by Companies (Accounting Standards) Rules, 2015, (“Indian Accounting Standards”) by and to the extent possible in the same format as that adopted by the Parent Company for its separate financial statements.

The Parent Company consolidates entities which it owns or controls. The consolidated financial statements comprise the financial statements of the Parent Company, its subsidiaries and its controlled trust as disclosed below. Control exists when the parent company has power over the entity, is exposed or has rights to variable returns from its involvement with the entity; and has the ability to affect those returns by using its power over the entity. Power is demonstrated through existing rights that give the ability to direct relevant activities, those which significantly affect the entity’s returns. Subsidiaries are consolidated from the date control commences until the date control ceases.
The standalone financial statements of the Parent Company, its subsidiary companies and its controlled trust have been combined on line by line basis by adding together the book values of like items of assets and liabilities, income and expenses after eliminating intra group balances and intra group transactions except where cost cannot be recovered. The unrealised profits or losses resulting from the intra group transactions and balances have been eliminated.

The excess of the cost to the Parent Company of its investment in a subsidiary and the Parent Company’s portion of equity of subsidiary on the date at which investment in the subsidiary is made, is described as goodwill and recognised separately as an asset in the consolidated financial statements. The excess of the Company’s portion of equity of the acquired company over its cost is treated as gain on bargain purchase in the consolidated financial statements. Goodwill arising on consolidation is not amortised. It is tested for impairment on a periodic basis and written off if found impaired.
The consolidated financial statements are prepared using uniform accounting policies for like transactions and other events in similar circumstances and necessary adjustments required for deviations, if any, are made in the consolidated financial statements. The consolidated financial statements are presented in the same manner as the Parent Company’s separate financial statements.
